content_md:
I've started Joyce Appleby's *The Relentless Revolution: A History of Capitalism*, and am enamored with her elevation of culture as the appropriate lens for interpreting capitalism (and other economic phenomena).

*Homo economicus* has always felt to be a precisely wrong model for thinking about human behavior—not only because it reduces human agency and behaviors to what the modeler chooses, but also because it's (dare I say) culturally chauvinist.

This question of culture and human values *is* the terrain that matters imo. 

I made a version of this argument in 2015, writing about Kissinger's *World Order*: the values the West calls "universal" are universalizable, but they are not universally held. *Homo economicus* makes the same mistake, treating one culture's assumptions as human nature.

I think this appreciation of culture and distinct value sets will increase in importance as our dependence upon AI grows.

Reading Michael Levin's *Artificial Intelligences: A Bridge Toward Diverse Intelligence and Humanity's Future*, I highlighted a passage for which this thread is an early response. In the margins, I wrote "This is a good idea for an essay." Perhaps I will write it.

> What skills and properties are essential to our humanity, and which are we willing to give up as we turn our finite attention to more interesting concerns?
